sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud computing provides computing resources and services over a network, commonly through provider-managed infrastructure.
bullets: Private, public, hybrid, and community cloud
IaaS, SaaS, and PaaS
Shared vs. dedicated resources
Metered utilization
Ingress and egress
Elasticity and availability
File synchronization
Multitenancy
sections.callout: WHO OWNS/USES IT? → WHAT SERVICE DO I RECEIVE? → HOW DOES THE CLOUD BEHAVE?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes who uses the cloud, how much the provider manages, how resources are consumed, or how services scale and share infrastructure, identify the matching cloud concept.
bullets: One organization → private cloud
Provider cloud open to many customers → public cloud
Private and public together → hybrid cloud
Organizations with common needs → community cloud
Rent infrastructure → IaaS
Use a finished application → SaaS
Deploy apps on a managed platform → PaaS
Pay based on consumption → metered utilization
Scale with demand → elasticity
Multiple customers share provider infrastructure → multitenancy

sections.title: Common Cloud Models
paragraphs: Cloud models describe who uses the environment and how much of the technology stack a provider manages. Deployment models answer who the cloud is for; service models answer what the provider delivers.
sections.callout: DEPLOYMENT MODEL = WHO? SERVICE MODEL = WHAT?

sections.title: Private Cloud
paragraphs: A private cloud is dedicated to a single organization. It may be hosted on-premises or by a third-party provider; the defining point is that the environment is dedicated to one organization.
sections.callout: Company wants cloud-style infrastructure reserved exclusively for itself → private cloud.

sections.title: Public Cloud
paragraphs: A public cloud is operated by a provider and offered to many customers. Customers consume services from the provider's infrastructure.
sections.callout: Business rents provider resources alongside many other customers → public cloud.

sections.title: Private vs. Public Cloud
sections.callout: ONE ORGANIZATION → PRIVATE. MANY CUSTOMERS → PUBLIC.

sections.title: Hybrid Cloud
paragraphs: A hybrid cloud combines private and public cloud environments. An organization might keep sensitive databases private while using public cloud resources for web workloads.
sections.callout: Private plus public working together → hybrid cloud.

sections.title: Community Cloud
paragraphs: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common requirements or interests, such as security, regulatory, industry, or mission requirements.
sections.callout: Related organizations with shared needs → community cloud.

sections.title: Cloud Service Models
paragraphs: Cloud service models classify how much of the technology stack the provider manages. Objective 4.2 requires Infrastructure as a Service, Software as a Service, and Platform as a Service.
sections.callout: How much of the technology stack does the customer manage?

sections.title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
paragraphs: IaaS provides foundational virtual compute, storage, and networking. The provider manages the physical infrastructure while the customer has more control over operating systems and workloads.
sections.callout: Cloud virtual machines while the customer manages the OS and applications → IaaS.

sections.title: Software as a Service (SaaS)
paragraphs: SaaS delivers a complete application. The provider manages most of the underlying technology while the user signs in, configures permitted settings, and uses the software.
sections.callout: Use the finished cloud application without managing servers → SaaS.

sections.title: Platform as a Service (PaaS)
paragraphs: PaaS provides a managed platform on which developers build and deploy applications. The provider manages the underlying infrastructure and operating environment while developers focus on code, data, and application configuration.
sections.callout: Bring your code; the provider manages the platform → PaaS.

sections.title: IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS
sections.callout: I = INFRASTRUCTURE. P = PLATFORM. S = SOFTWARE.

sections.title: Cloud Characteristics
paragraphs: Cloud environments have recognizable operational characteristics involving resource allocation, measurement, data movement, scaling, access, synchronization, and tenant separation.
bullets: Shared vs. dedicated resources
Metered utilization
Ingress/egress
Elasticity
Availability
File synchronization
Multitenancy

sections.title: Shared Resources
paragraphs: Shared resources are infrastructure resources used by multiple customers or workloads. Providers pool compute, storage, and networking capacity to use infrastructure efficiently.
sections.callout: Shared = underlying resources serve multiple users or customers.

sections.title: Dedicated Resources
paragraphs: Dedicated resources are reserved for a particular customer or workload. They can provide greater isolation, predictable resource access, or specialized performance and compliance characteristics.
sections.callout: Dedicated = reserved for you.

table.caption: Resource allocation
rows: Pool used by multiple customers or workloads
Assigned to one customer or workload

sections.title: Metered Utilization
paragraphs: Metered utilization means cloud consumption is measured. Customers may be charged based on compute time, storage, data transfer, and other service usage.
sections.callout: Monthly bill changes with resource consumption → metered utilization.

sections.title: Ingress
paragraphs: Ingress is data entering a cloud environment or service.
sections.callout: Uploading local data into cloud storage → ingress.

sections.title: Egress
paragraphs: Egress is data leaving a cloud environment or service.
sections.callout: Transferring cloud-hosted data out of the provider environment → egress.

sections.title: Ingress/Egress
sections.callout: Provider accounting or charges for data movement may depend on service terms.

sections.title: Elasticity
paragraphs: Elasticity is the ability to increase or decrease resources as demand changes, such as adding compute capacity during peak traffic and reducing it when demand falls.
sections.callout: Resources automatically stretch and shrink with demand → elasticity.

sections.title: Elasticity vs. Scalability
paragraphs: Scalability is closely related, but this objective specifically requires elasticity: resources can dynamically grow or shrink as demand changes.
sections.callout: DEMAND CHANGES → RESOURCES CHANGE.

sections.title: Availability
paragraphs: Availability describes whether a service or resource is accessible when needed. Redundancy, multiple systems or locations, and failover can improve availability.
sections.callout: Service remains accessible despite a component failure → availability.

sections.title: Availability vs. Performance
paragraphs: A service can be available but slow, or fast but occasionally unavailable. Availability asks whether it is up; performance asks how fast it operates.
sections.callout: AVAILABILITY = UP. PERFORMANCE = FAST.

sections.title: File Synchronization
paragraphs: File synchronization keeps copies of files updated across systems or devices. An edit on one device can make the updated version available on another synchronized device.
sections.callout: Keep copies aligned across devices → file synchronization.

sections.title: Synchronization vs. Backup
sections.callout: A deletion or change may also synchronize; synchronization is not automatically a backup.

sections.title: Multitenancy
paragraphs: Multitenancy means multiple customers, called tenants, use shared infrastructure while their environments and data remain logically separated.
sections.callout: Many customers, one underlying platform, logically separated → multitenancy.

table.caption: Related cloud concepts
rows: Separate customers use the shared environment

sections.title: Multitenancy vs. Public Cloud
paragraphs: A public cloud often uses multitenancy, but the terms are not identical. Public cloud is a deployment model; multitenancy is an architecture in which tenants share infrastructure while remaining logically isolated.
sections.callout: PUBLIC = WHO CAN USE IT. MULTITENANT = HOW CUSTOMERS SHARE IT.

sections.title: Objective 4.2 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Cloud questions often mix deployment models, service models, and operational characteristics. First identify which classification the scenario is testing.

entries.title: Private vs. Public
paragraphs: Private is dedicated to one organization; public provider services are offered to many customers.

entries.title: Hybrid vs. Community
paragraphs: Hybrid combines private and public environments; community serves organizations with common requirements.
entries.memoryHook: TWO CLOUD TYPES vs. RELATED ORGANIZATIONS

entries.title: IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS
paragraphs: IaaS supplies infrastructure, PaaS supplies a development platform, and SaaS supplies a finished application.
entries.memoryHook: BUILD THE SERVER → IaaS | BUILD THE APP → PaaS | USE THE APP → SaaS

entries.title: Shared vs. Dedicated
paragraphs: Shared resources are pooled; dedicated resources are reserved.

entries.title: Ingress vs. Egress
paragraphs: Ingress enters the cloud; egress exits the cloud.

entries.title: Metered Utilization vs. Elasticity
paragraphs: Metered utilization measures consumption; elasticity changes resources with demand.
entries.memoryHook: HOW MUCH USED? vs. HOW MUCH NEEDED NOW?

entries.title: Elasticity vs. Availability
paragraphs: Elasticity changes resource amount; availability keeps a service accessible.

entries.title: File Synchronization vs. Backup
paragraphs: Synchronization aligns current copies; backup preserves a recoverable copy.

entries.title: Multitenancy vs. Dedicated
paragraphs: Multitenancy supports multiple logically isolated customers on shared infrastructure; dedicated resources are reserved for one customer or workload.
entries.memoryHook: MANY TENANTS vs. ONE RESERVED RESOURCE

sections.title: Cloud Decision Path
bullets: Ask who owns or uses the environment to identify the deployment model.
Ask what the provider delivers to identify IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
Determine whether resources are shared or dedicated.
Identify whether the scenario concerns measured use, data direction, changing demand, uptime, file alignment, or tenant separation.
Apply the narrowest official term that matches the scenario.
sections.callout: WHO? → WHAT SERVICE? → WHAT BEHAVIOR?
